questions.question: What is RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) and why do Java backend teams use it?
questions.title: What Is RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) and Why Java Backend Teams Use It
questions.direct_answer: **RAG** is an architecture that improves LLM responses by fetching relevant documents from a knowledge base at query time and injecting them as context before calling the model. Instead of relying solely on what the model learned during training, you **retrieve** fresh, domain-specific text and **augment** the prompt with it. Java backend teams reach for RAG when they need answers grounded in their own data — product docs, support tickets, internal wikis — without retraining or fine-tuning a model. With Spring AI, the pipeline is: embed the user query → search a `VectorStore` (e.g. `PgVectorStore`) → attach top-k chunks → call the LLM via `QuestionAnswerAdvisor`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands RAG as an architecture pattern, not just a buzzword — specifically the retrieve-then-augment flow, why it beats hallucination-prone plain LLM calls, and what problem it solves without fine-tuning
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing RAG with fine-tuning — they're different levers. RAG is inference-time retrieval; fine-tuning is training-time weight adjustment. Also: describing RAG as just 'sending documents to the model' without understanding the vector-similarity retrieval step
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the hallucination-vs-staleness tradeoff — RAG helps with both by grounding answers in retrieved text. Discuss chunking, embedding model choice, and the fact that retrieval quality (recall) is the real bottleneck, not the LLM

sections.title: The Problem RAG Solves
sections.content:
LLMs are trained on a snapshot of the world. Ask a model about your internal product documentation, last week's incident report, or a proprietary API — it doesn't know. You have two options: retrain the model (expensive, slow, requires MLOps) or tell it what it needs to know at query time.

RAG takes the second path. Before calling the LLM, you **retrieve** the most relevant chunks of text from your own knowledge base and **augment** the prompt with them. The model now answers from evidence you supplied, not from vague training-time memory. Responses are more accurate, citations are possible, and you can update the knowledge base without touching the model.

The core flow:
1. **Ingest** — split documents into chunks, embed each chunk with an embedding model, store vectors in a vector database.
2. **Retrieve** — embed the user's question, find the top-k most similar chunks via cosine similarity.
3. **Augment** — prepend those chunks to the prompt as context.
4. **Generate** — call the LLM; it answers using both its training knowledge and your retrieved context.

sections.title: Why Java Backend Teams Specifically Reach for RAG
sections.content:
Java backend teams already own the data pipelines, REST APIs, and databases. RAG plugs naturally into that stack:

- **Spring AI 1.0.0-M6+** ships `VectorStore`, `PgVectorStore`, `EmbeddingModel`, `DocumentRetriever`, and `QuestionAnswerAdvisor` — you don't need Python tooling.
- **PostgreSQL + pgvector** is often already in the stack; `PgVectorStore` adds the vector search layer without a new database.
- **No model ownership** — the team calls an LLM API (OpenAI, Bedrock, Vertex) without managing GPU infrastructure.
- **Data stays internal** — documents never have to leave your VPC if you use a self-hosted embedding model and a local vector store.
- **Iterative improvement** — tuning retrieval (chunking, top-k, reranking) is a Java problem, not an ML problem.

sections.title: Spring AI RAG: The Four-Component Model
sections.content:
Spring AI models RAG around four concerns:

**1. EmbeddingModel** — converts text to a float vector. The same model must be used at ingest and at query time.

**2. VectorStore** — stores `Document` objects (text + metadata + embedding vector) and answers similarity queries. `PgVectorStore` backs this with PostgreSQL's `pgvector` extension.

**3. DocumentRetriever** — wraps a `VectorStore` and a `SearchRequest` (top-k, similarity threshold, metadata filters). Returns the most relevant `Document` list for a given query string.

**4. QuestionAnswerAdvisor** — a Spring AI `Advisor` that intercepts a `ChatClient` call, runs retrieval, injects the retrieved documents as a system context block, then lets the request flow to the LLM. You wire it in one line.

```java
@Bean
ChatClient ragChatClient(ChatClient.Builder builder, VectorStore vectorStore) {
    return builder
        .defaultAdvisors(new QuestionAnswerAdvisor(vectorStore))
        .build();
}
```

Calling `ragChatClient.prompt().user(question).call().content()` triggers the full RAG pipeline transparently.

sections.title: What RAG Doesn't Fix
sections.content:
RAG solves grounding; it doesn't solve everything:

- **Retrieval quality is the bottleneck.** If the top-k chunks don't contain the answer, the LLM can't conjure it. Bad chunking or the wrong embedding model hurts recall before the LLM even sees the prompt.
- **Context window limits.** You can inject only so many chunks before you hit the model's token limit. Reranking (pick the best 3 of the top 20) helps.
- **Hallucination isn't eliminated.** The model can still ignore your context or mix it with training noise. Prompt engineering and fact-checking mitigate but don't remove this.
- **Latency adds up.** A vector search + embedding call adds 50–300 ms before the LLM call starts. Profile end-to-end, not just LLM time.
- **Multi-hop reasoning is hard.** If answering requires connecting two documents the retriever returns separately, the LLM may miss the join.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **RAG = retrieve relevant chunks at query time, inject as context, then call the LLM.**
- **It's an inference-time pattern** — no model retraining or fine-tuning needed.
- **Spring AI 1.0.0-M6+** provides `VectorStore`, `PgVectorStore`, `EmbeddingModel`, `DocumentRetriever`, `QuestionAnswerAdvisor` — a full RAG stack in Java.
- **`QuestionAnswerAdvisor`** wires retrieval into `ChatClient` as an advisor — transparent to the calling code.
- **Retrieval quality drives answer quality** — chunking, embedding model, and top-k matter more than prompt tuning.
- **RAG vs fine-tuning:** RAG = fresh data at query time; fine-tuning = baked-in knowledge at training time.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
RAG is a pattern that grounds LLM responses in your own data without retraining the model.

**The core idea**
- LLMs only know what they saw at training time — they don't know your docs
- RAG fixes this by retrieving relevant text at query time and injecting it as context before calling the LLM
- The model answers from evidence you gave it, not from training-time guesses

**The four-step flow**
1. Ingest: chunk documents, embed each chunk, store vectors in a `VectorStore`
2. Retrieve: embed the user's question, find top-k similar chunks by cosine similarity
3. Augment: prepend those chunks to the prompt as context
4. Generate: call the LLM — it sees both training knowledge and your retrieved text

**Why Java teams like it**
- Spring AI ships `PgVectorStore`, `EmbeddingModel`, and `QuestionAnswerAdvisor` — no Python needed
- PostgreSQL with pgvector is often already in the stack
- No GPU infrastructure — you just call an LLM API

**The real caveat**
- Retrieval quality is the bottleneck — if top-k chunks don't contain the answer, the LLM can't invent it
- Hallucination drops but doesn't disappear
- Latency budget includes embedding + vector search before the LLM call starts

questions.question: RAG vs fine-tuning — when do you use each approach?
questions.title: RAG vs Fine-Tuning — When to Use Each LLM Customization Approach
questions.direct_answer: **RAG** retrieves relevant context at inference time from an external knowledge base — no model weight changes. **Fine-tuning** adjusts model weights on your domain data during a training run. Use **RAG** when your data changes frequently, you need citations, or you want to keep the base model's broad reasoning. Use **fine-tuning** when you need a different response style, domain-specific vocabulary the model consistently gets wrong, or latency is critical and you can't afford retrieval. Most Java backend teams start with RAG — it's cheaper, faster to iterate, and doesn't require MLOps infrastructure. Fine-tuning is additive: you can RAG on top of a fine-tuned model for the best of both.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands these as complementary levers, not mutually exclusive choices — and knows specifically when each approach's properties (freshness, latency, cost, style control) matter
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating fine-tuning as 'better' because it sounds more sophisticated. In practice, fine-tuning doesn't help with knowledge freshness and is expensive to redo. Many teams fine-tune for style, then layer RAG for fresh facts
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss the combined approach — fine-tune for tone and domain vocabulary, then RAG for current facts. Mention that fine-tuning on factual knowledge often leads to confident hallucinations, while RAG anchors to retrieved evidence

sections.title: Two Different Levers for the Same Goal
sections.content:
Both RAG and fine-tuning customize LLM behavior for your domain. They're not the same lever, and picking the wrong one wastes time and money.

**RAG** works at **inference time** — you don't touch the model. Before each LLM call, you retrieve relevant text from your knowledge base and inject it as context. The model's weights stay frozen. Changes to your data are instantly reflected — no retraining cycle.

**Fine-tuning** works at **training time** — you adjust the model's weights on a curated dataset of examples. The result is a model that behaves differently (different tone, vocabulary, format) without needing retrieval at call time. But it requires a training run, labeled data, and iteration whenever behavior drifts.

They're not mutually exclusive. A fine-tuned model with RAG on top gets the consistent style and vocabulary from fine-tuning plus fresh, grounded facts from retrieval.

sections.title: RAG vs Fine-Tuning — Side by Side
sections.content:
| Aspect | RAG | Fine-Tuning |
|---|---|---|
| When it works | Inference time (every call) | Training time (once, then deployed) |
| Knowledge freshness | Instant — update the vector store | Stale — requires a new training run |
| Requires MLOps | No — just a vector DB and an embedding model | Yes — GPU compute, data curation, evaluation |
| Response style control | Limited — the base model's style dominates | High — you can shape tone, format, vocabulary |
| Hallucination risk | Lower — answer is grounded in retrieved text | Higher — confident hallucinations on new facts |
| Latency impact | +50–300ms for embedding + retrieval | None at inference time |
| Cost to iterate | Low — swap chunks, re-embed, done | High — full or partial training run |
| Best for | Frequently changing data, citations, knowledge Q&A | Consistent style, domain jargon, structured output format |
| Java tooling | Spring AI `VectorStore`, `QuestionAnswerAdvisor` | Off-stack — Python training pipelines typically |

sections.title: When to Pick RAG
sections.content:
**Reach for RAG when:**

- **Data changes frequently** — product docs, support tickets, news. You can't retrain every day.
- **You need citations** — RAG can return the source chunks; fine-tuning can't tell you where it learned something.
- **You want grounded answers** — hallucination risk drops because the model has retrieved evidence in front of it.
- **You lack MLOps capacity** — Spring AI's `PgVectorStore` and `QuestionAnswerAdvisor` run in your existing Java stack with no GPU.
- **You need multi-domain coverage** — one base model plus domain-specific vector stores per domain is cheaper than many fine-tuned models.
- **You're prototyping** — RAG pipelines are up in hours; fine-tuning cycles take days.

RAG is the right starting point for most Java backend teams building knowledge-grounded features.

sections.title: When to Pick Fine-Tuning
sections.content:
**Reach for fine-tuning when:**

- **You need consistent output format** — structured JSON, a specific markdown schema, a brand voice. Prompt engineering alone is fragile; fine-tuning makes it reliable.
- **Domain vocabulary is a constant problem** — the base model consistently misunderstands domain-specific terms (medical codes, legal abbreviations, proprietary product names).
- **Latency is critical** — fine-tuning eliminates the retrieval round-trip. If you need sub-100ms LLM responses, removing the vector search helps.
- **Data is stable** — if your domain knowledge doesn't change often, the retraining cost amortizes well.
- **You want a smaller model to match a larger one** — fine-tuning a 7B model on expert examples can match a 70B base model on narrow tasks.

**Don't fine-tune to inject facts.** Fine-tuning a model on factual Q&A doesn't make it more accurate — it makes it more confidently wrong. RAG is the right tool for facts.

sections.title: The Combined Approach and Real-World Patterns
sections.content:
**Fine-tuning + RAG together:**
- Fine-tune for **style, format, and vocabulary** — the model learns to produce the output shape you need.
- Layer RAG on top for **current facts** — the fine-tuned model's style shines; RAG's retrieved context provides the substance.
- This combination is common in enterprise deployments: fine-tuned model for the persona, RAG for the knowledge base.

**What most Java teams actually do:**
1. Start with RAG on a base model (Spring AI + PgVectorStore). Ship it.
2. Discover format or style issues. Add system prompt engineering.
3. If style is still inconsistent at scale, consider a targeted fine-tuning run for format.
4. Never fine-tune for facts — keep RAG handling that.

**Cost reality check:**
- RAG iteration: engineer time only. No compute bill for retraining.
- Fine-tuning: labeled data curation (expensive human time) + GPU compute + evaluation pipeline. Budget accordingly.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **RAG = inference-time knowledge injection; fine-tuning = training-time weight adjustment.**
- **Use RAG** for fresh data, citations, grounded answers, and fast iteration without MLOps.
- **Use fine-tuning** for consistent output format, stable domain vocabulary, and latency-critical paths.
- **Never fine-tune to inject facts** — it produces confident hallucinations, not accuracy.
- **They're complementary** — fine-tune for style, RAG for substance.
- **Most Java teams start with RAG** — Spring AI makes it a same-stack operation.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
These are two different levers for customizing an LLM. They're complementary, not competing.

**RAG — inference-time knowledge injection**
- You retrieve relevant docs from your knowledge base before each LLM call
- The model's weights don't change — data freshness is instant
- Lower hallucination risk because the model sees retrieved evidence
- No GPU or MLOps required — Spring AI handles it in your Java stack
- Best for: frequently changing data, knowledge Q&A, citation needs

**Fine-tuning — training-time weight adjustment**
- You train the model on curated examples to change how it behaves
- Expensive to redo when data changes — needs a new training run
- Best for: consistent output format, domain vocabulary, latency-critical paths
- Terrible for injecting facts — fine-tuned factual knowledge hallucinates confidently

**The decision heuristic**
- Data changes? RAG. Style is inconsistent? Fine-tuning. Both? Use them together — fine-tune for format, RAG for facts.

**Java team reality**
- Start with RAG. It ships fast, iterates cheap, and lives in your existing stack. Add fine-tuning only when RAG can't fix the specific problem you're seeing.

questions.question: How do you implement a RAG pipeline with Spring AI and PGVector?
questions.title: Implementing a RAG Pipeline with Spring AI and PGVector — Embed, Retrieve, Inject, Generate
questions.direct_answer: A Spring AI RAG pipeline has two phases. **Ingestion:** load documents, split into chunks with `TokenTextSplitter`, embed each chunk via `EmbeddingModel`, and store into `PgVectorStore`. **Query:** embed the user's question, run vector similarity search via `DocumentRetriever` or directly via `VectorStore.similaritySearch()`, inject top-k chunks as system context, then call the LLM. Spring AI's `QuestionAnswerAdvisor` automates the query phase — wire it into `ChatClient.Builder.defaultAdvisors()` and the full retrieve-augment-generate cycle runs per request. The underlying database needs the `pgvector` extension and a `VECTOR(1536)` column — `PgVectorStore` creates this automatically in Spring AI 1.0.0-M6.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the actual mechanics — not just the concept but the concrete Spring AI classes and the two-phase ingestion/query split. Can they wire VectorStore, EmbeddingModel, and QuestionAnswerAdvisor correctly?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing only the query phase and forgetting ingestion entirely. Also: not knowing that the same EmbeddingModel must be used in both phases, or thinking the vector store is optional
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the token budget problem — you can only inject so many chunks before hitting the context window. Discuss metadata filters, similarity thresholds in SearchRequest, and async batch ingestion for large document sets

sections.title: Two Distinct Phases: Ingest Once, Query Many Times
sections.content:
A RAG pipeline splits into two phases with very different operational properties.

**Ingestion** happens offline (or asynchronously): you load documents, split them into chunks, embed each chunk with an `EmbeddingModel`, and store the resulting vectors in `PgVectorStore`. This is a write-heavy batch operation — run it when documents are created or updated. Ingestion quality determines the ceiling for retrieval quality; no amount of prompt tuning fixes poor chunking.

**Query** happens per user request: embed the question with the same `EmbeddingModel`, search `PgVectorStore` for the top-k most similar chunks, inject those chunks as context into the prompt, then call the LLM. Spring AI's `QuestionAnswerAdvisor` automates this entire sequence — your controller just calls `chatClient.prompt().user(q).call().content()`.

The critical constraint: **ingestion and query must use the same embedding model**. Mix them and cosine similarity comparisons become meaningless — retrieval silently breaks with no error.

sections.title: Phase 1: Document Ingestion
Phase 2: RAG Query with QuestionAnswerAdvisor
Advanced: Metadata Filters and Similarity Thresholds
sections.content:
The default `SearchRequest.defaults()` returns top 4 chunks without a similarity floor. For production, tune it:

```java
SearchRequest searchRequest = SearchRequest.query(userQuestion)
    .withTopK(6)
    .withSimilarityThreshold(0.75)   // drop irrelevant chunks
    .withFilterExpression("category == 'java' && version >= 17"); // metadata filter
```

Metadata filters require that your documents carry those metadata fields at ingest time:
```java
var doc = new Document(
    chunkText,
    Map.of("category", "java", "version", 21, "source", "spring-docs")
);
vectorStore.add(List.of(doc));
```

`PgVectorStore` translates filter expressions into SQL `WHERE` clauses against a JSONB `metadata` column — no extra infrastructure needed.

**Token budget:** 6 chunks × 300 tokens each = 1,800 tokens of context. With a 4K context window model you're at 45% capacity before the user's question. Monitor prompt token counts in production and add a `withTopK` ceiling if you're near the model's limit.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Two phases:** ingest (offline) and query (per-request). Use the **same `EmbeddingModel` for both**.
- **Ingestion flow:** `PagePdfDocumentReader` → `TokenTextSplitter` → `VectorStore.add()`.
- **Query flow:** `QuestionAnswerAdvisor` handles embed → search → inject automatically when wired into `ChatClient.Builder.defaultAdvisors()`.
- **`PgVectorStore`** backs the vector store with PostgreSQL + pgvector; auto-creates schema in dev (`initialize-schema: true`).
- **`SearchRequest`** controls `topK`, `similarityThreshold`, and metadata filters — tune all three for production.
- **Token budget matters** — each injected chunk consumes context window; cap `topK` based on chunk size and model limit.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A Spring AI RAG pipeline splits into two phases — ingest documents once, query on every user request.

**Ingestion phase**
- Load documents with a reader like `PagePdfDocumentReader`
- Split into chunks with `TokenTextSplitter`
- Call `vectorStore.add(chunks)` — `PgVectorStore` embeds each chunk via `EmbeddingModel` and stores the vector in PostgreSQL
- The schema (pgvector extension + vector_store table) auto-creates in development

**Query phase — what QuestionAnswerAdvisor does for you**
1. Intercepts the ChatClient call before it hits the LLM
2. Embeds the user's question via the same EmbeddingModel
3. Runs cosine similarity search on PgVectorStore, returns top-k documents
4. Injects those documents as a system context block in the prompt
5. Forwards the augmented request to the LLM

**Wiring it up**
- Add `QuestionAnswerAdvisor` to `ChatClient.Builder.defaultAdvisors()` — one line in a `@Configuration` bean
- Your controller just calls `chatClient.prompt().user(question).call().content()`

**Production tuning**
- `SearchRequest.withTopK(6)` and `.withSimilarityThreshold(0.75)` filter out irrelevant chunks
- Metadata filters on `SearchRequest` limit retrieval to a document subset without a separate index
- Watch token budget — 6 chunks × 300 tokens each eats 1,800 context tokens before the question lands

questions.question: What chunking strategies exist for RAG document ingestion, and how do they affect retrieval quality?
questions.title: RAG Chunking Strategies for Document Ingestion — How Chunk Size and Overlap Affect Retrieval Quality
questions.direct_answer: Chunking splits documents into segments that get independently embedded and stored. The strategy directly controls what the vector search retrieves. **Fixed-size token chunking** (Spring AI's `TokenTextSplitter` with 512-token chunks, 100-token overlap) is the safe default — fast and predictable. **Sentence/paragraph chunking** preserves semantic units; better for prose-heavy docs. **Hierarchical chunking** stores parent+child: embed small child chunks for precision retrieval, but return the larger parent context to the LLM. **Semantic chunking** groups sentences by embedding similarity shift — highest quality but slowest to ingest. Chunk size trades off recall vs precision: small chunks improve embedding accuracy but may miss multi-sentence context; large chunks capture more context but dilute the embedding signal.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands that chunking is a critical design decision, not a boilerplate step — and specifically how chunk size and overlap interact with embedding quality and context window budget
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating chunking as 'just split at N tokens' without thinking about semantic boundaries. Also: not knowing the chunk-size vs embedding-quality tradeoff, or thinking bigger chunks are always better because they contain more information
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe hierarchical (parent-child) chunking — the insight that retrieval precision and LLM context size are separate concerns. Also mention the practical effect of chunk overlap on sentence-boundary queries

sections.title: Why Chunking Strategy Matters More Than Most Teams Expect
sections.content:
Every document that enters a RAG pipeline gets split into chunks — and each chunk gets its own embedding vector. That embedding represents the semantic meaning of that chunk. When a user asks a question, you compare the question's embedding against all chunk embeddings and retrieve the most similar ones.

The chunk is the atomic unit of retrieval. If important context spans two chunks, retrieval may return one but not the other. If a chunk is too long, the embedding averages out too many concepts and becomes a weak signal. If it's too short, there's not enough context to answer the question even when you retrieve the right chunk.

Chunking is a design decision, not a boilerplate step. The strategy you pick determines the ceiling of your retrieval quality — no amount of prompt engineering or LLM ability fixes poor chunking.

sections.title: Strategy 1: Fixed-Size Token Chunking (Spring AI Default)
Strategy 2: Sentence and Paragraph Chunking
Strategy 3: Hierarchical (Parent-Child) Chunking
Strategy 4: Semantic Chunking
The Chunk Size vs Retrieval Quality Tradeoff
sections.content:
**Small chunks (128 tokens):**
- Precise embeddings — the vector represents one narrow idea
- High retrieval precision — you find exactly what you're looking for
- Low context richness — the LLM gets a fragment; may not have enough to answer fully
- More chunks to search — larger vector index, slower search

**Large chunks (1024+ tokens):**
- Diluted embeddings — the vector blurs together many ideas
- Lower retrieval precision — you retrieve the right section but also irrelevant parts
- High context richness — the LLM has more to work with
- Fewer chunks — faster search, but less selective

**Overlap's role:**
- Prevents sentence-boundary misses — a query about a sentence that straddles chunk borders can match either chunk
- 10–20% overlap is a practical default; higher overlap increases index size proportionally

**Practical starting point:** 512 tokens, 100-token overlap, `TokenTextSplitter`. Profile retrieval quality (manually check top-5 results for 20 test queries). Adjust chunk size before reaching for semantic chunking.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Chunking is a design decision** — it determines the ceiling of RAG retrieval quality.
- **Fixed-size token chunking** (`TokenTextSplitter`) is the safe default — fast, predictable, supported natively in Spring AI.
- **Sentence/paragraph chunking** is better for prose documents; worse for mixed-format technical docs.
- **Hierarchical chunking** decouples retrieval precision (small child chunks) from LLM context richness (larger parent chunks) — best balance for technical documentation.
- **Semantic chunking** gives highest quality but is expensive at ingest; usually only worth it for high-stakes domains with slow-changing docs.
- **Chunk size tradeoff:** smaller = precise embeddings, less context; larger = diluted embeddings, more context. **Overlap** prevents sentence-boundary misses.
- **Start at 512 tokens + 100-token overlap**. Tune after profiling retrieval quality, not before.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Chunking is how you split documents before embedding. It's the most underrated part of the RAG pipeline — bad chunking breaks retrieval before the LLM ever sees the question.

**Fixed-size token chunking (Spring AI default)**
- `TokenTextSplitter` with 512-token chunks and 100-token overlap
- Fast, predictable, good enough for most structured documents
- Weakness: splits mid-sentence; overlap partially compensates

**Sentence and paragraph chunking**
- Split at natural language boundaries — semantically coherent
- Better for prose-heavy docs where paragraphs are self-contained ideas
- Variable chunk size makes token-budget planning harder

**Hierarchical (parent-child) chunking**
- Small child chunks (128 tokens) for precise embedding and retrieval
- Larger parent chunks (512 tokens) returned to the LLM for context richness
- Decouples retrieval precision from answer context — best balance for technical docs

**Semantic chunking**
- Detect topic shifts by measuring cosine similarity drops between consecutive sentence embeddings
- Highest quality chunks — each one represents a single coherent concept
- Expensive at ingest time — embedding every sentence before splitting

**The core tradeoff**
- Small chunks: precise embeddings, low context richness
- Large chunks: diluted embeddings, high context richness
- Overlap prevents sentence-boundary misses — use 10–20% of chunk size as overlap

**Practical advice**
- Start at 512 tokens + 100-token overlap. Run 20 manual test queries, check top-5 retrieval results, and adjust chunk size based on what you find. Reach for semantic or hierarchical strategies only when the simpler approach has a documented quality gap.

familiarity_anchors: each chunk gets its own embedding — the chunk is the atomic unit of retrieval

speakable_v2.standard_example: TokenTextSplitter at 512 tokens with 100-token overlap — query about a sentence near a chunk boundary still gets retrieved because it appears in both adjacent chunks
speakable_v2.hook: Chunking looks like boilerplate. It's not. How you split documents sets the ceiling for everything the LLM can do with your knowledge base.

beats.text: You're optimising for retrieval precision vs context richness. Small chunks give focused embeddings — higher precision. Large chunks give the LLM more to work with. Your strategy picks where you land on that tradeoff.

groups.heading: Fixed-size token chunking
groups.text: Spring AI's TokenTextSplitter at 512 tokens with 100-token overlap. Fast, simple, predictable. Good default. Weakness: can split mid-sentence.

groups.heading: Sentence and paragraph chunking
groups.text: Split at natural language boundaries. Each chunk is a coherent unit. Better for prose. Weakness: variable chunk sizes complicate token budget planning.

groups.heading: Hierarchical parent-child chunking
groups.text: Embed small child chunks for precise retrieval, but return larger parent chunks to the LLM for context. Decouples the two concerns. Best balance for technical docs.

groups.heading: Semantic chunking
groups.text: Detect topic shifts by measuring cosine similarity drops between consecutive sentences. Highest quality. Expensive at ingest — you embed every sentence before splitting.

beats.text: Start with TokenTextSplitter at 512 tokens and 100-token overlap. It's in Spring AI and it's enough to prove the pipeline works. Move to hierarchical if top-k misses the right section. Use semantic chunking only for high-stakes, slow-changing knowledge bases.

beats.label: Signals you have the wrong strategy
items: If top-k returns the right section but the wrong paragraph, chunks are too large
If the LLM says it lacks context even when the answer is in the knowledge base, chunks are too small
If quality is still poor after tuning top-k and threshold, move to semantic or hierarchical chunking

speakable_v2.cap: Chunking strategy determines retrieval quality, and retrieval quality determines answer quality. Start simple, measure retrieval with real queries, and move to a more expensive strategy only when you've seen a specific gap.
